title: Merkel Cells: Touch Receptors That Are Not Neurons

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: Two touch afferents fire when a probe starts moving. During a motionless hold, one keeps firing and the other falls silent. Which better fits an SA1 response, and why?
cards.back: The afferent that keeps firing. SA1 responses persist during a hold; rapidly adapting responses mainly track skin movement.
cards.quote: Some of the nerve fibres from that skin fire only while the skin is moving.

cards.front: A {{c1::Merkel cell-neurite complex}} pairs a basal epidermal Merkel cell with a contacting Aβ low-threshold afferent terminal.
cards.quote: A Merkel cell-neurite complex is a Merkel cell in the basal epidermis together with the terminal of an Aβ low-threshold afferent that contacts it.
cards.section: An epithelial cell that feels force

cards.front: What does the description “Aβ low-threshold afferent” imply about the axon and its stimulus?
cards.back: A large, myelinated, fast-conducting sensory axon that light touch can excite.
cards.quote: Aβ fibres are large, myelinated, fast-conducting axons, and low-threshold means that light touch is enough to excite them.
cards.section: An epithelial cell that feels force

cards.front: What did embryonic mouse lineage tracing establish about Merkel-cell origin, despite their neuronal appearance?
cards.back: Merkel cells arise from epidermal progenitors; their contacting afferent is a sensory neuron derived from neural crest.
cards.quote: But genetic lineage tracing in mouse embryos (Van Keymeulen and colleagues, 2009) showed that Merkel cells arise from epidermal progenitors.
cards.section: An epithelial cell that feels force

cards.front: During a held skin indentation, what is the dynamic phase of an SA1 response?
cards.back: The high-frequency burst at the onset of the press.
cards.quote: a burst that reports the onset, then irregular firing that lasts as long as the press.
cards.section: The signature response: a burst, then a hold

cards.front: During a held skin indentation, what is the static phase of an SA1 response?
cards.back: Continued firing during the hold, with irregular intervals between spikes.
cards.quote: a burst that reports the onset, then irregular firing that lasts as long as the press.
cards.section: The signature response: a burst, then a hold

cards.front: A touch response that starts at onset, continues into the hold, and stops before release is {{c1::intermediately adapting}}.
cards.quote: A response that fires through the onset and into the hold, but stops before the press ends, is called intermediately adapting.
cards.section: The signature response: a burst, then a hold

cards.front: In hypothetical held-touch recordings, silencing a receptor-cell route changes onset firing from 200 to 180 Hz and hold firing from 30 to 6 Hz. Calculate each percentage loss and identify the more affected phase.
cards.back: Onset loss = (200 − 180)/200 × 100 = 10%. Hold loss = (30 − 6)/30 × 100 = 80%. The hold is more strongly affected.
cards.quote: Here the two phases are two measurements, and the question is which cell makes each.
cards.section: The signature response: a burst, then a hold

cards.front: In the two-receptor model for mouse touch domes, how do the ending and Merkel cell contribute to SA1 firing?
cards.back: The ending’s own transduction mainly carries onset. Merkel-cell Piezo2 transduction and transmitter release mainly sustain the hold; the division is not exclusive.
cards.quote: The split is a matter of which input dominates each phase, not an exclusive division.
cards.section: Two receptors, one axon

cards.front: Why can recording spikes from a sensory axon fail to distinguish direct force sensing by its ending from input supplied by a contacting receptor cell?
cards.back: Both routes converge on the same axon. Selectively perturbing one route helps separate their contributions.
cards.quote: Both routes converge on one axon, so a recording from the nerve mixes them.
cards.section: Two receptors, one axon

cards.front: A mouse line expressing Cre recombinase under a particular promoter is a {{c1::Cre driver}}.
cards.quote: A Cre driver is a mouse line that makes the enzyme Cre recombinase under a particular promoter.
cards.section: Two receptors, one axon

cards.front: What did Woo’s cultured newborn-mouse Merkel-cell recordings show after epithelial Piezo2 deletion?
cards.back: Mechanically activated currents were undetectable in all 13 recorded Merkel cells, supporting a requirement for epithelial Piezo2 in those currents.
cards.quote: When Piezo2 was deleted from skin epithelium, none of 13 cultured Merkel cells had a detectable mechanically activated current.
cards.section: Two receptors, one axon

cards.front: A Krt14-Cre Piezo2 deletion abolishes cultured Merkel-cell mechanical currents while afferents retain Piezo2. Why would calling this a Merkel-cell-specific knockout overstate the experiment?
cards.back: Krt14-Cre acts throughout the epidermal lineage. The recordings test Merkel-cell currents, but effects elsewhere in epithelium are not excluded.
cards.quote: The epithelial driver is not specific to Merkel cells, so the deletion removes the channel from the whole epidermal lineage, and only the Merkel cells were recorded.
cards.section: Two receptors, one axon

cards.front: In Maksimovic’s ex vivo mouse skin-saphenous nerve preparation, light-driven Merkel-cell activation evokes SA1 spikes without touch. What causal claim does this support?
cards.back: Merkel-cell activation is sufficient to evoke afferent firing, given the targeting controls. It does not by itself establish necessity during touch.
cards.quote: Driving the cells tests whether they are sufficient to make the afferent fire.
cards.section: Two receptors, one axon

cards.front: During a held touch in an ex vivo mouse touch dome, targeted light silencing suppresses sustained afferent firing. What does this establish that light activation alone cannot?
cards.back: An acute requirement for the Merkel-cell route in normal sustained firing. Activation alone tests sufficiency; silencing during touch tests necessity in the moment.
cards.quote: Silencing them during a touch tests whether they are needed in the moment (acute necessity).
cards.section: Two receptors, one axon

cards.front: Mouse touch-dome epithelium loses Piezo2 while the afferent ending retains it. Under the two-receptor model, what happens to onset versus held-touch firing, and why?
cards.back: Onset should remain relatively preserved, while normal sustained firing is lost or reduced: the ending retains transduction, but the Merkel-cell transduction route is impaired.
cards.quote: In mouse touch domes, the afferent ending's own transduction mainly carries the onset of a touch.
cards.section: Two receptors, one axon

cards.front: In mouse touch domes, epithelial Piezo2 deletion leaves onset firing similar to controls, but developmental Atoh1 deletion removes Merkel cells and reduces onset. Why can neither result assign an exclusive onset mechanism?
cards.back: The manipulations differ: removing cells also removes possible support beyond their Piezo2 current and may alter development. Neither removes the ending’s transduction. The stated model assigns dominance, not exclusivity, so onset can still receive both inputs.
cards.quote: Atoh1 loss is developmental, so it cannot say what the cells do acutely in an adult.
cards.section: Two receptors, one axon

cards.front: Blocking epidermal vesicle release with tetanus toxin reduces both phases of mouse touch-dome firing. What does this suggest about release and onset?
cards.back: Epidermal release, probably from Merkel cells, contributes to onset as well as the hold. The manipulation does not isolate the Merkel cell’s acute contribution.
cards.quote: So release from the epidermis, probably from Merkel cells, matters for the onset too, though neither manipulation isolates the Merkel cell's acute contribution.
cards.section: Two receptors, one axon

cards.front: After developmental Merkel-cell loss in mice, mean peak SA1 firing is 79 Hz versus 238 Hz in controls. Calculate the remaining fraction and percentage reduction.
cards.back: Remaining = 79/238 = 0.332, or 33.2%. Reduction = (238 − 79)/238 = 0.668, or 66.8%. These are ratios of group means.
cards.quote: Peak SA1 firing was 79 ± 40 Hz in the knockouts and 238 ± 69 Hz in controls (mean ± SD).
cards.section: Worked problem: how much does losing Merkel cells cost the dynamic phase?

cards.front: A ratio of knockout and control group means is 0.332. Why does that not show that every recorded afferent retained 33.2% of its original firing?
cards.back: Separate group means do not measure changes within individual afferents. Variation within each group can be substantial.
cards.quote: Scope of the number: this is a ratio of two group means, not the change within any one afferent.
cards.section: Worked problem: how much does losing Merkel cells cost the dynamic phase?

cards.front: A receptor-current record has a mean peak of 370 pA and a mean steady level of 20 pA. Calculate the steady-to-peak ratio of means as a percentage.
cards.back: Steady/peak = 20/370 = 0.0541, about 5.4%. This is a ratio of means, not an average of individual-cell ratios.
cards.quote: As a ratio of the two group means, the steady current is 20/370, about 5.4% of the peak.
cards.section: A brief current that holds a press

cards.front: In a thought experiment, a 370 pA peak decays exponentially to 20 pA with an 8 ms time constant, and that steady current lasts 1 s. Estimate each component’s charge and the steady share.
cards.back: Transient excess: (370 − 20) pA × 0.008 s ≈ 2.8 pC. Steady: 20 pA × 1 s = 20 pC. Steady share ≈ 20/(20 + 2.8) × 100 = 87.7%, about 88%.
cards.quote: For a transient that decays exponentially, it is about amplitude × time constant, once the hold is much longer than the time constant.
cards.section: A brief current that holds a press

cards.front: How can a small steady receptor current help sustain firing when a much larger initial peak is brief?
cards.back: The peak’s charge leaks away. A continuing current can maintain depolarization, allowing voltage-gated calcium channels to respond throughout the hold.
cards.quote: What a steady current does is hold a steady depolarization for as long as it flows, and voltage-gated calcium channels respond to voltage.
cards.section: A brief current that holds a press

cards.front: For illustration, impose a constant 20 pA on a passive membrane with an assumed input resistance of 1 GΩ. What is its steady voltage change?
cards.back: ΔV = IR = (20 × 10⁻¹² A)(1 × 10⁹ Ω) = 0.020 V = 20 mV above rest. The resistance is assumed, not measured in Merkel cells.
cards.quote: For illustration only, imposing a constant 20 pA on a passive membrane with an assumed input resistance of 1 GΩ
cards.section: A brief current that holds a press

cards.front: Why can the passive-membrane calculation for an imposed 20 pA not predict the voltage of a Merkel cell whose Piezo2 current was 20 pA in voltage clamp?
cards.back: An imposed current stays fixed, whereas a Piezo2 current changes as depolarization reduces its driving force. The stated voltage-clamp caveat requires resting potential, reversal potential and membrane conductances to predict the real cell’s voltage.
cards.quote: The measured 20 pA came from voltage clamp, so predicting the real cell's voltage needs its resting potential, the channel's reversal potential and its conductances.
cards.section: A brief current that holds a press

cards.front: The coefficient of variation of interspike intervals equals their {{c1::standard deviation divided by their mean}}.
cards.back: A CV of zero indicates perfectly regular intervals.
cards.quote: The coefficient of variation (CV) of the interspike intervals is their standard deviation divided by their mean
cards.section: A brief current that holds a press

cards.front: A noise-free fixed-threshold integrate-and-fire model fires regularly under steady drive. Replace that drive with randomly timed transmitter packets. What happens to regularity, and why is an exact CV unjustified?
cards.back: Firing can become irregular because input arrives at variable times. The exact CV depends on packet statistics and the spike generator; random release alone does not specify it.
cards.quote: Randomly timed packets can make firing irregular, but the CV depends on the packet statistics and on the spike generator.
cards.section: A brief current that holds a press

cards.front: An investigator claims irregular firing during held touch proves randomly timed transmitter release from receptor cells. What alternative mechanism must be considered, and what conclusion is justified?
cards.back: A branched sensory ending with several spike-initiation sites can add irregularity. The stated alternative means irregular firing is consistent with synaptic input, but cannot identify release statistics or prove that release caused the irregularity.
cards.quote: a branched ending with several spike-initiation sites, contacting many Merkel cells, can add irregularity of its own.
cards.section: A brief current that holds a press

cards.front: Why is finding action potentials in a skin cell insufficient to classify it as a neuron?
cards.back: Non-neuronal cells can fire calcium spikes. Excitability alone does not establish neuronal identity.
cards.quote: Excitability does not make them neurons: many non-neuronal cells fire calcium spikes.
cards.section: A different reading from rat whiskers

cards.front: Ikeda patch-clamped Merkel cells inside excised rat whisker follicles. Depolarization-evoked spikes survived tetrodotoxin but vanished with cadmium. What mechanism does this support?
cards.back: Calcium-dependent spikes: cadmium blocks voltage-gated calcium channels, whereas tetrodotoxin did not block these spikes.
cards.quote: Tetrodotoxin did not block the action potentials evoked by depolarizing the cell, and cadmium, which blocks voltage-gated calcium channels, abolished them.
cards.section: A different reading from rat whiskers

cards.front: In an excised rat whisker follicle, cadmium eliminates static afferent firing and most dynamic firing while stopping Merkel-cell calcium spikes. Can this localize the calcium dependence to Merkel cells?
cards.back: No. Cadmium can reach calcium channels in other cells. The stated drug-access limit means the result supports calcium-channel dependence of both phases in this preparation, but cannot assign each necessary step to a particular cell.
cards.quote: Cadmium applied to the follicle can reach any cell in it.
cards.section: A different reading from rat whiskers

cards.front: Why need Ikeda’s rat whisker findings and the mouse touch-dome two-receptor model not assign identical roles to Merkel cells?
cards.back: The preparations differ, and follicle-wide cadmium cannot localize calcium dependence. The source of onset firing remains disputed.
cards.quote: A rat whisker follicle is also not a mouse touch dome, so a difference between this paper and the mouse papers could be a difference of preparation.
cards.section: A different reading from rat whiskers

cards.front: In the macaque texture recordings, what feature scale was represented spatially by SA1 firing?
cards.back: Millimetre-scale features. Fine texture was carried by the timing of RA and PC responses in that texture set.
cards.quote: In this texture set, SA1 firing represented millimetre-scale features spatially, and fine texture was carried by the timing of RA and PC responses.
cards.section: What SA1 input is for

cards.front: A tactile system uses SA1 spatial firing for millimetre-scale patterns and RA/PC timing for fine texture. If RA/PC timing is disrupted while SA1 spatial signals remain, which judgment should suffer more, and why?
cards.back: Fine-texture judgment should suffer more, because its timing code is disrupted; the stated spatial code for millimetre-scale patterns remains available.
cards.quote: In this texture set, SA1 firing represented millimetre-scale features spatially, and fine texture was carried by the timing of RA and PC responses.
cards.section: What SA1 input is for

cards.front: Researchers record a texture code in SA1 afferents without manipulating their contacting Merkel cells. Why does this not establish that Merkel cells are necessary for that code?
cards.back: Recording identifies information carried by the afferents. Necessity requires perturbing the Merkel-cell contribution and testing the effect.
cards.quote: Those recordings measured afferents and did not manipulate Merkel cells, so they show what SA1 fibres carry, not what Merkel cells are needed for.
cards.section: What SA1 input is for

cards.front: Which three transmitter accounts are proposed for Merkel-cell signalling, and in which principal preparations?
cards.back: Noradrenaline: mouse touch domes. Serotonin: mouse whiskers. Protons acting through afferent ASICs: rodent whisker complexes. Transmitter identity remains unsettled.
cards.quote: What is released is the open problem. Three accounts say what, and each rests on its own preparation.
cards.section: The synapse nobody agrees on: noradrenaline, serotonin or protons

cards.front: Mechanically triggered serotonin release and receptor-blocker effects in mouse whiskers are offered as proof of a universal Merkel-cell serotonin transmitter. What other evidence prevents that conclusion?
cards.back: The reported release method cannot distinguish serotonin from noradrenaline. Touch-dome afferents were not excited by serotonin, and whisker fast EPSCs survived a 5-HT3 blocker. The stated preparation and endpoint differences prevent a universal transmitter conclusion.
cards.quote: that serotonin did not excite touch-dome afferents, and that the release method used cannot tell serotonin from noradrenaline.
cards.section: The synapse nobody agrees on: noradrenaline, serotonin or protons

cards.front: What does an excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) measure at a receptor-cell–afferent synapse?
cards.back: The current evoked by transmitter in the afferent, measured without passing through spike generation.
cards.quote: the current that transmitter evokes in the afferent, without passing through spike generation.
cards.section: The synapse nobody agrees on: noradrenaline, serotonin or protons

cards.front: In rodent whisker complexes, a β2 blocker leaves touch-evoked fast EPSCs unchanged, while ASIC3 deletion diminishes them. What does this imply about a proposed fast β2-mediated signal?
cards.back: The results argue against β2 receptors carrying the fast EPSC in that preparation and support an ASIC contribution. They do not exclude a slower adrenergic effect.
cards.quote: That argues against β2 carrying the fast EPSC at whisker complexes, though not against a slower adrenergic effect.
cards.section: The synapse nobody agrees on: noradrenaline, serotonin or protons

cards.front: Design a test that distinguishes site-specific from time-scale-specific β2 and ASIC3 contributions to Merkel-cell signalling while addressing developmental deletion confounds.
cards.back: Compare same-age mouse touch domes and whiskers with acute adult afferent-specific deletions of each receptor, measuring fast EPSCs and slow modulation. The stated alternatives predict site-restricted effects versus β2-dependent slow and ASIC3-dependent fast effects at both sites. Block Merkel-cell release as a common dependency test.
cards.quote: Then ask separately about fast EPSCs and slower modulation, since a β2 receptor and a proton-gated channel could each act on a different time scale.
cards.section: Design problem
